notes.meaning: Naaman was the top commander of the Aramean army, highly respected by his king and famous for winning great battles. Scripture points out that the Lord, the true God of Israel, was the one who gave Aram victory through him. Even with all his wealth and honor, Naaman suffered from a terrible skin disease called leprosy. His situation shows that earthly success cannot protect anyone from deep trouble and physical weakness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars point out that the ancient Hebrew term for leprosy covered various serious skin diseases, rather than modern Hansen's disease.

notes.meaning: Aramean raiding parties had invaded Israel and captured a little girl, who was put to work serving Naaman's wife. Even though she was taken away from her homeland as a captive, she held onto her faith in the Lord. God used this painful trial in her life to set up a great work of healing and mercy.

The servant girl told her mistress that if Naaman would only visit the prophet living in Samaria, he would be cured of his disease. Samaria was the capital city of Israel, where God's prophet Elisha lived. Her simple, caring advice showed great faith that God's prophet could heal what no doctor could cure.

Naaman went directly to his master, the king of Aram, and reported what the young Israelite captive had told his wife. Even though the news came from a lowly slave girl, Naaman took her words seriously because he was desperate for help. God often uses the quiet words of the humble to reach people in high places.

The king of Aram told Naaman to go at once and gave him an official letter of introduction to the king of Israel. Naaman packed an enormous fortune of silver, gold, and ten fine changes of clothes as a royal gift. In ancient times, people brought rich gifts when asking a ruler or prophet for help, and the king assumed Israel's monarch could arrange the cure.

The letter brought by Naaman asked the king of Israel to cure the general of his dreaded skin disease. The Aramean king assumed that Israel's king had direct authority over any prophet in the land and could simply command the miracle. But because the letter did not name Elisha, it sounded like an impossible royal demand.

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his robes in sheer panic and cried out that only God has the power over life and death to heal a leper. Tearing clothes was a traditional sign of deep grief or shock. He suspected the Aramean king was making an impossible request just to pick a fight and start a war.

When Elisha heard that the king had torn his clothes in fear, he sent a message telling him to calm down and send Naaman to him. Elisha wanted the foreign general to see firsthand that the living God had a true prophet in Israel. The prophet stepped forward so that God's power, rather than royal panic, would define the moment.

Naaman rode up to Elisha's home in a grand display of chariots, horses, and soldiers, stopping right outside the door. He came as an important foreign leader and expected the prophet to come out and welcome him with honor. He waited outside, expecting a reception worthy of his high rank.

Instead of greeting Naaman personally, Elisha sent a servant out with simple instructions to wash seven times in the Jordan River to be fully cleansed. Elisha stayed inside to show that the miracle was entirely God's work, not a show put on for a powerful guest. The command called for simple, humble obedience from a proud warrior.

Naaman stormed away furious because Elisha did not even step outside to greet him. He had pictured the prophet coming out, calling on the Lord, and waving his hand over the diseased skin in an impressive ceremony. Human pride often wants a grand spectacle instead of God's quiet, simple ways.

Naaman angrily protested that the Abanah and Pharpar, the clean mountain rivers of Damascus, were far better than all the waters of Israel. He felt insulted by the order to wash in the Jordan and marched away in a rage, ready to go home without help. He failed to see that healing would come from God's power, not the quality of the river water.

Naaman's servants approached him with deep respect and urged him to reconsider his anger. They gently pointed out that if the prophet had demanded some difficult, heroic feat, he would have done it without hesitation. Since the prophet only asked him to do something simple and wash, he had every reason to try it.

Naaman listened to his servants, went down into the Jordan River, and dipped himself seven times just as the prophet had directed. When he came up the seventh time, his disease was gone, and his skin was as healthy and smooth as that of a young child. God rewarded his humble obedience and made him completely whole.

Naaman and his whole entourage returned to Elisha, walked into his presence, and openly declared that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. He then begged the prophet to accept a lavish reward as an expression of his deep gratitude. His physical healing led to a true change of heart and faith in the one living God.

Elisha swore by the living Lord that he would not take any payment or gift, refusing even when Naaman repeatedly urged him. Elisha wanted to make sure Naaman knew that God's grace and healing are free gifts that cannot be bought with money. He guarded God's glory by refusing to profit from the miracle.

When Elisha refused the gift, Naaman asked for as much soil from Israel as two mules could carry. He vowed that he would never again offer a sacrifice to any idol, but only to the Lord. In ancient times, people believed that worshipping a nation's God required building an altar on dirt taken from that God's own land.

Naaman asked the Lord to forgive him for one difficult duty when he returned home. His aging king would lean on his arm when entering the temple of the Syrian god Rimmon, forcing Naaman to bow as the king bowed. Naaman wanted God to know that his heart belonged only to the Lord, even when his official royal duties required him to bow physically.

Elisha answered Naaman with the traditional blessing, 'Go in peace,' sending him on his way with God's goodwill. The prophet did not lay heavy burdens on the new believer, trusting the Lord to continue guiding his conscience. Naaman then departed and began his journey home.

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, watched Naaman leave and resented that his master had let the Aramean go without taking any of his wealth. He swore an oath that he would chase after Naaman and get something for himself. Greed tempted Gehazi to undo the pure, free witness Elisha had just given.

Gehazi hurried after Naaman, and when the general saw him running, he stepped down from his chariot to greet him with great respect. Naaman asked with concern if everything was all right, fearing some trouble had happened to Elisha. His generous courtesy showed how much he truly honored God's prophet.

Gehazi lied to Naaman, claiming that two young prophets had unexpectedly arrived from the hill country of Ephraim in need of help. He asked for a talent of silver and two sets of clothes on their behalf, pretending his master had sent the request. He disguised his own greedy desires under the excuse of charity for others.

Naaman was delighted to help and insisted that Gehazi take two talents of silver instead of one, along with two fine changes of clothes. He tied the heavy silver into two bags and had two of his own servants carry them ahead of Gehazi. Naaman gave gladly and generously, completely unaware that he was being tricked.

When they reached the hill near Samaria, Gehazi took the bags from Naaman's servants and hid the treasure safely inside his house. He then dismissed the men so that his secret would remain hidden. He believed he had gotten away with his scheme and that no one would ever find out.

Gehazi went in and stood before Elisha to carry out his daily duties as if nothing had happened. When Elisha asked him where he had been, Gehazi told another blatant lie, saying he had not gone anywhere. Dishonesty had quickly piled upon greed, hardening his heart against the truth.

Elisha revealed that his spirit had been with Gehazi in a prophetic vision when Naaman stepped down from the chariot to meet him. He asked Gehazi whether this was an appropriate time to chase after money, fine clothes, land, and servants when God's honor was at stake. Elisha exposed both the lie and the selfish dreams Gehazi had secretly planned to buy.

Elisha announced God's judgment, declaring that Naaman's leprosy would cling to Gehazi and his family line forever. Gehazi left the prophet's presence covered in skin disease as white as snow. He gained silver and clothes, but lost his health, his calling, and his honor before God.
